pages.name: Slopes at 1, 2 and 3 s
pages.text: The speeding boat again: `f(x) = x²` metres after `x` seconds. P sits on its graph with the dashed tangent, whose slope is the number the chords from P settle on: 2 m per s at 1 s, 4 at 2 s and 6 at 3 s. Each slope drops a dot on the graph below, at the same `x` and as high as the slope. Drag P along the curve to drop more.

pages.name: The slope at 4 s
pages.task: P is now at `4 s`, where `f(4) = 16 m`. Chords from P read `0.81 ÷ 0.1 = 8.1 m per s` over `0.1 s`, and `0.0801 ÷ 0.01 = 8.01` over `0.01 s`. How high will P's dot sit on the graph below?
pages.why: The chords read 8.1 and 8.01, each above 8 by its gap, so they settle on 8. The slope at 4 s is 8 m per s, and P's dot sits at 8, in line with 2, 4 and 6. The 16 m is how far the boat has gone.

pages.name: A rule for every x
pages.text: Sweep P along the whole graph and its dots line up on a straight line through zero that rises 2 for every 1 across. So at `x` seconds the boat is doing `2x` metres per second. That rule is a function in its own right, the [[derivative]] of f, written `f′(x)` and read 'f dash of x' (many books say 'f prime'). Put in a time, `x`, and it gives back the slope there.

pages.name: At 5 s
pages.task: The dots follow `f′(x) = 2x`. P is at 5 s. How fast is the boat going at that moment, the height of P's dot below?
pages.why: `f′(5) = 2 × 5 = 10` m per s, so P's dot sits at 10, on the line. 25 m is f(5), how far the boat has gone, and `5 + 2 = 7` adds where `2x` multiplies.

pages.name: Why 2x: a growing square
pages.text: Why `2x`? `x²` is `x × x`, the area of a square of side `x`. Grow the side by a small step `h` and the new square is the old one plus two strips, each `x` by `h`, and a corner `h` by `h`: a growth of `2xh + h²`. That is how far `y = x²` climbs from `x` to `x + h`, so the chord's slope is the growth ÷ `h`. Each strip, `x` by `h`, divided by `h` leaves `x`, and the corner, `h` by `h`, divided by `h` leaves `h`, so the slope is `2x + h`. Shrink `h`: at `x = 3` it reads 7, 6.5, 6.1 and 6.01, settling on 6.

pages.name: A side of 5
pages.task: A square of side 5 grows by `h = 0.1`. Its two strips add `2 × 5 × 0.1 = 1` and its corner `0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01`. What is the slope of the chord on `y = x²` from 5 to 5.1, the growth ÷ `h`?
pages.why: The growth is `1 + 0.01 = 1.01`, and `1.01 ÷ 0.1 = 10.1`. That is `2x + h` at `x = 5`: 10 plus the step itself, so it settles on 10 as `h` shrinks.

pages.name: Left of zero
pages.text: Now the plain curve `y = x²`, from −3 to 3. Left of zero it falls as `x` grows, so its slopes there are below zero, and the dots carry on along the same line, below the axis: `f′(−2) = 2 × −2 = −4`, though the curve itself is at 4. At 0 it is flat at the bottom, and `f′(0) = 0`. The square needed a side above zero, but `(x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h²` holds for any `x`.

pages.name: The slope at −1
pages.task: On the plain curve, P sits at `x = −1`, where the curve is at 1. The dots follow `f′(x) = 2x`. What is `f′(−1)`?
pages.why: `f′(−1) = 2 × −1 = −2`. The curve is falling there, so P's dot sits below the axis, on the line. That does not put the curve, or its tangent, through (−1, −2): the curve is at (−1, 1), and −2 is how steeply it falls.

pages.name: The cable drum
pages.task: An example cable drum pays out `f(x) = 3x` metres of cable after `x` seconds. Which rule gives the slope of its graph at every `x`?
pages.why: The graph is a straight line climbing 3 m every second, so the tangent at every point is the line itself, with slope 3. The derivative is the flat line `f′(x) = 3`: 3 m per s at every moment, not `3x`, which is f itself.

pages.name: A growing plate
pages.task: An example square plate has a side of 20 cm, and the side is growing. How fast is its area growing, per cm of side?
pages.why: Each small step `h` adds two strips, each 20 cm by `h`, plus a corner that shrinks away, so the area grows at `2 × 20 = 40` cm² per cm of side: `f′(x) = 2x` at `x = 20`. 400 cm² is the area itself, and 20 counts one strip.

pages.name: A new curve
pages.task: This curve is `y = x² − 2x`, and its derivative is `f′(x) = 2x − 2`. P sits at `x = 3`. What is the slope there, the height of P's dot below?
pages.why: `f′(3) = 2 × 3 − 2 = 4`, so the tangent at P climbs 4 for every 1 across, and P's dot sits at 4, on the line `2x − 2`. 3 is where the curve is, and 6 forgets the − 2.
